Q1: Author's argument is that GI Bill/VA housing benefits were distributed unequally by race via local policy choices. Option 0 (Levittown barred Black buyers, veterans included) directly supports. Option 2 (Shelley v. Kraemer) is about courts not enforcing covenants—tangential, doesn't support the argument of exclusion as well. Answer 0.

Q2: Option 1 weakens most directly. Answer 1.

Q3: Housing shortage—answer 2.

Q4: Shrinking tax bases/concentrated poverty—answer 3.

Audit: Stimulus facts—GI Bill 1944, VA loan guarantees with low/no down payment, FHA appraisal practices rating Black/mixed neighborhoods as poor risks, builders' racial covenants—all accurate. Fictional county figures are clearly labeled fictional. Options accurate: Levittown 1947 and exclusion of Black buyers; Shelley v. Kraemer 1948; Highway Act 1956. Distractor Q3[3] says the interstate "first allowed workers to commute by car"—wrong, but that's a distractor. Everything sound.

flags.detail: The petition says Omaha-to-Chicago is 'five times the distance' of Buffalo County (Kearney)-to-Omaha. Kearney to Omaha is roughly 190 rail miles; Omaha to Chicago roughly 470-490, about 2.5 times. Minor, and plausibly petitioner exaggeration, but presented as fact in a composed source; consider 'more than twice the distance.' Everything else (Wabash decision Oct. 1886, pending Interstate Commerce bill Jan.-Feb. 1887, Kearney in Buffalo County, rebates, long-haul/short-haul discrimination) checks out.

flags.detail: Option [3] credits the Northwest Ordinance (1787) with setting up 'a system for surveying western land.' The rectangular survey system was established by the Land Ordinance of 1785; the Northwest Ordinance governed territorial government and statehood admission. Minor conflation in a distractor, but the description is historically imprecise.

Q1: 0. Q2: 1 (vagrancy laws / hiring out directly supports convict leasing and coercion). Q3: 2 (Redeemer governments; convict leasing expanded under them). Q4: 3.

Audit: Stimulus is accurate on crop-lien, convict leasing, vagrancy convictions. "States leased prisoners ... paid the state a fee" — accurate. Q3 option 1 Great Migration is anachronistic as a distractor but that's fine; distractors are meant to be wrong. Q3 "expanded most directly" — crop-lien/sharecropping emerged during Reconstruction (before Redeemers), but convict leasing expanded notably under Redeemers, and the stem says "expanded," so defensible. No real problems.

Q1: 0. Q2: 1. Q3: 2. Q4: 3 (Half-Way Covenant 1662).

Checks: Q4 option 0 — the Massachusetts School Law of 1647 (towns of 50 households hire a schoolmaster) predates the letter, so it's a sound distractor. Dominion of New England 1686 — outside the decade. Rhode Island charter 1663 — within the decade but not caused by these concerns. Headright description accurate for Virginia. Stimulus consistent with Half-Way Covenant context; "forty pounds" plausible. Half-Way Covenant permitted baptism of children of baptized but unconverted parents — option wording "baptized nonmembers" is acceptable shorthand (they were "half-way" members). No real problems.

flags.detail: Option 1 (de facto lifelong servitude in the 1640s predating the statutes) best modifies the claim that law gave slavery its shape, but option 2 (planters' turn to enslaved labor after Bacon's Rebellion, the Morgan thesis) can also be defended as showing social/economic rather than legal forces drove racialization. The stem's 'most directly modify' leaves room for both; consider sharpening the stem or revising option 2.

"From Virginia to Massachusetts, assemblies refused to vote governors permanent salaries" — Virginia is a poor example: its royal governor's salary was paid from a permanent revenue (the two-shillings-per-hogshead tobacco export duty) established in the 1680s, so the Virginia burgesses did not withhold a permanent salary. The salary fight was characteristic of Massachusetts, New York, and others, not Virginia. Replace Virginia with New York or South Carolina.

content.text: Checking facts: Iraq invaded Kuwait August 2, 1990 — correct. UN Resolution 678 set January 15, 1991 deadline — correct. Congress voted January 12, 1991, before the air campaign began January 17 — correct. Coalition included Britain, Egypt, Saudi Arabia — correct. USSR did not veto — correct. Yellow ribbons as a 1991 symbol — accurate. The stimulus is clearly labeled fictional. Q3 option 0 is a distractor (USSR dissolved December 1991, after February 1991) — intentional. Q2 option 1: ground war ended Feb 28, 1991 after Kuwait liberated — accurate. Option 3's no-fly zones lasted until 2003 — accurate. Q4 option 0 is a chronology distractor (War Powers Resolution 1973). All sound.

Audit notes: The stimulus is sound. "Since the days of Jackson" is a reasonable reformer's rhetorical framing (spoils system popularly dated to Jackson); the "two percent" assessment matches documented party assessments; "the tragedy of the summer before last" (July 1881 Garfield shooting) is correctly dated relative to February 1883; the Pendleton Act (signed Jan. 16, 1883) initially covered roughly 10% of federal positions. Q2 option 1 is a minor simplification — Hayes suspended Arthur and Cornell in 1878 after the Senate had blocked removal in 1877 — but it is accurate enough for the stem's purpose. Q4 option 3 reflects the standard textbook claim that loss of assessments pushed parties toward corporate funding; turnout did not fall sharply in the 1880s, so option 0 is clearly wrong. No real problems to flag.

Stimulus audit: Portuguese on Gold Coast by 1480s (Elmina 1482) ✓; Madeira sugar with enslaved labor ✓; São Tomé settled 1480s–90s, sugar developed early 1500s — "by the 1480s... shipping them to sugar estates on Madeira and São Tomé" is slightly early for São Tomé but a minor compression. Taíno collapse ✓; royal licenses (asientos) ✓; New Laws 1542 effect ✓; Brazil largest destination by late 1500s ✓. Fictional author clearly labeled. Nothing serious.

flags.detail: Excerpt A explicitly describes antislavery petitions sent to Congress, so the gag rule (option 2) is the most direct consequence of that activism. The stem's '1840s' seems intended to exclude it (first gag adopted 1836), but the House made the gag a standing rule (Rule 21) in January 1840 and renewed it until 1844, so 'adoption of the House gag rule' in the 1840s is historically defensible. A student could reasonably choose option 2 over the Liberty Party; consider changing the stem's framing or the distractor's wording (e.g., 'the 1836 adoption').

Audit: The stimulus is clearly labeled as composed and the author is fictional. Details are accurate: $10/$5 commissioner fee differential, no testimony by the accused, no jury trial, affidavit of claimant sufficient, California admitted free in 1850, and petition for repeal. Booth held the opposite; no repeal until 1864). No real problems found.

flags.detail: Speech is dated January 8, 1833, yet the speaker says Jackson has 'twice this year' acted, referring to the July 1832 Bank veto and December 1832 Nullification Proclamation; these occurred in the previous calendar year ('this past year' would be consistent). Also, Jackson did not 'strike down the charter' in July 1832—he vetoed a recharter bill; the existing charter ran until 1836. Minor, and plausibly partisan hyperbole, but the chronology slip is an internal inconsistency.
